# Use Claude to Pull Out the Key Points of a Long Research Paper

> **In short:** Upload a research paper PDF to Claude and ask for a plain-English summary in five short sections. You'll need a Claude account and the PDF file; the whole thing takes about ten minutes.

Research papers are dense by design — they're meant to be read carefully and argued with, not skimmed on a Tuesday afternoon. Claude, the chat assistant from Anthropic, is unusually good at reading long documents and pulling out the bones of what's actually being said. This guide walks you through turning any academic PDF into a clean, structured summary you can actually use, whether you're a student trying to understand a paper for class, a journalist scanning sources, or a professional keeping up with research in your field.

## Before you start
- A free Claude account at **claude.ai** (a paid plan unlocks more file uploads and longer documents — check Anthropic's site for current plan details).
- The research paper saved as a PDF on your computer or phone. Most journal articles have a free author copy on the author's university page or on repositories like PubMed Central.
- About 10 minutes.

## Step 1 — Open Claude and start a fresh chat
Open **claude.ai** in your browser, or launch the Claude mobile app, and sign in. If you don't have an account yet, the sign-up button is right at the top of the page — you'll need an email address and a password. Once you're in, look for a button labeled **"New chat"** (or a **+ icon**) and click it. A blank conversation screen opens with an empty message box at the bottom.
💬 Example: N/A — no typing in this step.
You'll know it worked when you see a clean, empty chat with no previous messages and a text box ready at the bottom of the screen.

## Step 2 — Attach the PDF
Click the **paperclip icon** 📎 next to the message box. A file picker opens; browse to your PDF, select it, and confirm. On mobile, the same paperclip opens your phone's file or photos app — pick **"Files"** or **"Documents,"** not photos. If you can't spot a paperclip, look for a **+ plus icon** or a button that says **"Add file"** or **"Upload"** — Claude offers the same feature under slightly different labels depending on the device and platform. After you select the file, its filename appears as a small chip just above the text box.
💬 Example: N/A — no typing in this step.
You'll know it worked when the PDF's filename is visible as a label or chip above the message box, before you've typed anything.

## Step 3 — Ask for a structured five-section summary
Click into the message box and type a clear, specific prompt asking for the summary in five labeled parts. Then send it — press Enter on a computer, or tap the upward arrow on mobile. You'll see a small "thinking" indicator for a few seconds while Claude reads the PDF, and then its reply appears. The reply should be longer than a chat message — usually several short paragraphs with headings or numbered points.
💬 Example: "Please summarize this paper in plain English using five short sections: (1) the main question the research tries to answer, (2) the method they used, including who or what they studied, (3) the key findings, (4) what the authors conclude, and (5) the limits of the study the authors mention. Keep each section to 2–4 sentences."
You'll know it worked when Claude's reply breaks into labeled sections that match what you asked for — usually with bold headings, numbered items, or clear paragraph breaks.

## Step 4 — Ask follow-up questions on the parts that confuse you
Stay in the same chat and type a question about something in the summary that didn't quite land — a method, a term, a number, anything. Press Enter. Claude replies with a focused answer because it still has the full PDF in memory and the previous summary right in front of it. This is where Claude really earns its keep: you don't have to re-upload or re-explain. If the first answer is still fuzzy, ask a sharper follow-up, like "Can you give me a concrete example?" or "What does that mean in everyday language?"
💬 Example: "In section 2 you mentioned 'a randomized controlled trial with 240 participants' — can you explain in plain words what that actually means they did, step by step?"
You'll know it worked when Claude's reply addresses that one specific question and references details from the paper rather than answering in general terms.

## Step 5 — Copy or export the summary for later
Hover over Claude's reply and look for a small **copy icon** (usually two overlapping squares) in the corner of the message — click it and the entire reply lands on your clipboard, ready to paste into a note, an email, or a Google Doc. If you don't see a copy icon, click and drag to highlight the text manually, then press Ctrl+C (or Cmd+C on a Mac). For the full conversation history, look for a **download or share** option in the chat's menu — Claude can export the whole thread as a text or PDF file. One honest note: Claude can summarize well, but it can miss nuances, misread a graph caption, or smooth over a contradiction the authors are actually arguing about, so use the summary as a map, not the territory.
💬 Example: N/A — no typing in this step.
You'll know it worked when you can switch to another app and paste the summary cleanly, or when a downloaded file appears in your downloads folder.

## Common mistakes
- **Asking for "a summary" without specifying the format.** Claude will give you something, but it will often be one wall of paragraph text. Always tell it the structure you want — sections, length, audience — because it's dramatically better at filling a template than guessing what you meant.
- **Forgetting to check that the PDF actually uploaded.** If you typed your prompt and sent it without seeing a file chip above the box, Claude is answering from its general knowledge, not from the paper. Scroll up, look for the filename, and re-attach if it's missing.
- **Trusting the summary as a substitute for the paper.** For anything important, spot-check the original section Claude points you to. The summary is a map; the paper is the territory, and the map can drop landmarks.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** When a news article cites a study and you want to know what it actually said — without paying $40 for the journal — drop the free PDF into Claude and get a five-section summary in two minutes, enough to decide whether it's worth your evening.
- **For your business or work:** If you review research, write literature reviews, or build products grounded in evidence, this turns an afternoon of skimming into a quick first pass. You still need to read the key papers yourself, but Claude handles the long tail of "is this worth my time?" decisions.
- **If you're just getting started:** Open Claude right now and pick the shortest paper you can find — a two-page report or even a one-paragraph abstract works for practice. Ask for the same five-section summary and see how Claude structures the answer.

## Try it now
Find any open-access research paper (try Google Scholar with the PDF filter, or browse PubMed Central), upload it to Claude, and paste the example prompt from Step 3. You'll have a structured summary in under two minutes — and you'll know whether the paper deserves a closer read.
